Let $M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ represent a memory buffer where each row $\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is a k-sparse vector 

$$ \|\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{0} \leq k, \quad \text{for } i=1,2,\ldots m.$$

Given $M$, we define the associated sparsity matrix, $S\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$, by

$$ S_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } M_{ij} \neq 0, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} $$

The sparsity matrix $S$ allows us to ask queries like 'return a list of rows with a given sparsity pattern'. Let $\mathbf{q}\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ be a sparsity pattern, then we can simply do $\mathbf{a} = S\mathbf{q}$ where

$$a_{i} = | \text{supp}(\mathbf{v}_{i})\cap \text{supp}(\mathbf{q}) | \quad \text{for }i=1,2,\ldots,m.$$

The count $a_{i}$ on its own is not yet an answer; it becomes one once we fix a rule for what counts as a match. Writing $t = \|\mathbf{q}\|_{0}$ for the number of features the query asks about, we can define different rules for retrieval of memories:

- **overlap**, $a_{i} \geq \tau$. The memory shares at least $\tau$ of the queried features. This is the loosest rule: it tolerates memories that are missing some of what we asked for, and ranking by $a_{i}$ gives a graded notion of similarity rather than a yes/no answer.

- **containment**, $a_{i} = t$. Every feature in the query is present in the memory, i.e. $\text{supp}(\mathbf{q}) \subseteq \text{supp}(\mathbf{v}_{i})$. Since $a_{i}$ can never exceed $t$, saturating the count is exactly the condition that nothing was missed. The memory is free to carry extra features beyond the ones we asked for.

- **exact**, $a_{i} = t = \|\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{0}$. Containment, plus the memory has no features outside the query, so the two supports coincide. The extra condition costs nothing to check: the row weights $\|\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{0}$ are just the entries of $S\mathbf{1}$, which we can compute once and cache.

So a single matrix-vector product, together with a precomputed vector of row weights, is enough to answer all three.

## Clustering

The matrix $MM^{T}\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{m}$ is dot product between memories. 

Want to look at the idea of hierarchical graphs with nodes at higher levels representing clusters at finer resolution. See if can get a result where can have sublinear retrieval by starting at the coarse level and working our way down. Using clique tree representation of chordal graphs is appealing. Having some dynamics where we add and prune clusters as new cliques emerge. Can imagine doing this by having a threshold distance between points and consider different levels of this threshold to get coarser or finer graphs.
